results.claim: For p not dividing the base b, collision detection is exactly repeated-state detection on mismatch-only normalized prefix sums. Moreover, every collision has a witness containing at most p mismatching aligned positions, although its length may exceed p.
results.proof_sketch: Use the convention F(i,L)=sum_{t=0}^{L-1} s[i+t]b^{L-1-t} mod p. For displacement d define A_d(k)=sum_{t=0}^{k-1}(s[t]-s[t+d])b^{-(t+1)} mod p for 0<=k<=n-d. For r<e, multiplying A_d(e)-A_d(r) by b^e gives F(r,e-r)-F(r+d,e-r). Thus the two substrings collide exactly when A_d(r)=A_d(e) and the interval contains an actual mismatch. Let q_1<...<q_m be the mismatch positions between S[0..n-d) and S[d..n), and retain only B_0=0 and B_j=A_d(q_j+1). The state is constant between mismatches, so a true collision exists at displacement d iff two B_j are equal. A repeated pair B_a=B_c with a<c directly supplies unequal colliding substrings. If m>=p, the first p+1 states lie in F_p and two coincide; hence a collision with at most p mismatches exists. If m<p, every interval already has fewer than p mismatches.

results.claim: In the word-RAM model with p=n^{O(1)}, there is an exact deterministic algorithm running in O(n log n+n+min{D,M,n min(n,p)}) time, where D is the number of distinct substring contents and M is the number of unequal unordered character-position pairs. Consequently the requested O(n log n) bound holds when p=O(log n), D=O(n log n), or M=O(n log n).
results.proof_sketch: First build suffix-array/LCP/RMQ support for constant-time LCE queries. For every displacement d, LCE jumps enumerate only the m_d mismatch positions. Update the normalized state from the preceding claim and record (d,state,boundary). Stop after p mismatches: p+1 states force a collision. Otherwise enumerate all mismatches. Sorting the records by (d,state) detects repeated states exactly. There are Q<=n+sum_d min(m_d,p) records. Since sum_d m_d=M=(n^2-sum_c n_c^2)/2 and sum_d min(n-d,p)=O(n min(n,p)), Q=O(n+min{M,n min(n,p)}). Word-sized keys permit constant-pass radix sorting. Independently, a compact suffix tree has one explicit or implicit locus per distinct substring and total edge-label length D. Traversing edge labels character-by-character computes every distinct substring fingerprint in O(D); radix-sort the (length,fingerprint) pairs. A duplicate pair is exactly a collision because each content occurs once. Compute D during preprocessing and choose the cheaper route. If S has period q, each length has at most q distinct contents, so D<=nq; in particular q=O(log n) gives O(n log n). All these algorithms have zero error probability.

results.claim: Let C_L be the number of distinct length-L substring contents. After deterministic suffix-tree preprocessing, all values C_L can be computed in O(n) additional time; if C_L>p for any L, an unequal colliding pair can be constructed in O(n) additional word-RAM time. Thus every such instance has an exact O(n log n) solution, including instances outside the parent’s aggregate D- and M-bounded regimes.
results.proof_sketch: Trim suffix-tree leaf edges at the text boundary. An edge whose parent and child have string depths a<c contains exactly one character-boundary locus, hence one distinct substring content, at every length L in (a,c]. Conversely every distinct substring content is represented by exactly one such locus. Range-adding one on [a+1,c] for every edge and taking prefix sums computes the full profile C_1,...,C_n in O(n). If C_L>p, more than p distinct contents map into the p residues of F_p, so the strict pigeonhole principle guarantees an unequal collision. To construct it, filter the suffix array to suffixes of length at least L, use exact LCP queries between consecutive eligible suffixes to assign length-L content-class IDs, compute every length-L fingerprint by prefix arithmetic, and radix-sort complete (fingerprint,class,start) records. A fingerprint bucket containing two class IDs supplies the pair. There are at most n records. If no C_L exceeds p, this certificate makes no conclusion and the preceding adaptive detector is used. In particular, D=sum_L C_L>np is a sufficient trigger.

results.claim: The target has a complete O(n log n) exact solution in the noninvertible case p divides b.
results.proof_sketch: With the most-significant-character-first convention, b=0 mod p makes every nonempty fingerprint equal to its last character modulo p. For an endpoint e, let R_e=s[e]s[e-1]...s[0]. For endpoints e<f having the same final-character residue, no collision between their substrings is possible exactly when R_e is a prefix of R_f; otherwise, if their longest common suffix has length t<e+1, the two length-(t+1) substrings ending at e and f are unequal but have the same fingerprint. Group endpoints by final-character residue and consider each group in increasing endpoint order. It suffices to test consecutive endpoints because the prefix relation is transitive. LCS queries are LCP queries in the reversed string and can be preprocessed in O(n log n), after which all tests take O(n). For the opposite polynomial-coefficient convention, reverse the roles of first and last characters.

results.claim: Collisions cannot occur at length L when b^L<=p, but checking only power-of-two lengths, only lexicographically adjacent contents, or relying on monotonicity in the length is insufficient.
results.proof_sketch: Distinct canonical base-b words of length L represent integers whose nonzero difference has magnitude at most b^L-1; if b^L<=p, that difference cannot be divisible by p. For the limitations, take b=2, p=5, and S=000101. The fingerprint arrays by length are: L=1: [0,0,0,1,0,1]; L=2: [0,0,1,2,1]; L=3: [0,1,2,0]; L=4: [1,2,0]; L=5: [2,0]; L=6: [0]. Repeated hashes at lengths 1 and 2 correspond only to equal contents. At length 3, 000 and 101 have integer values 0 and 5 and collide. Every other length is collision-free. Thus all power-of-two lengths 1,2,4 pass, and collision existence is not monotone. At length 3 the lexicographically ordered distinct contents have values 0,1,2,5, so the sole colliding pair is nonadjacent.

results.claim: Under the most-significant-character-first convention, for the binary string S_m=0^m1^m and any odd prime p, an unequal equal-length fingerprint collision exists if and only if the multiplicative order ord_p(2) is at most m.
results.proof_sketch: Every length-L content occurring in S_m consists of L-j zeros followed by j ones for some allowed j. Its fingerprint is h_j=2^j-1 mod p. For j>k, h_j=h_k exactly when 2^k(2^{j-k}-1)=0 mod p, equivalently ord_p(2) divides j-k. At any fixed length the possible j-values span an interval of width at most m. Therefore ord_p(2)>m excludes every unequal collision. Conversely, if r=ord_p(2)<=m, the length-m substrings 0^m and 0^{m-r}1^r both occur, are unequal, and have fingerprints 0 and 2^r-1=0 mod p. Reversing the string gives the corresponding statement for the opposite coefficient convention.

results.claim: For every m>=1 there is an odd prime p=O(m^2 log(m+2)) satisfying ord_p(2)>m; hence the collision-free family S_m=0^m1^m uses permitted polynomial-size primes in the invertible, superlogarithmic regime.
results.proof_sketch: An odd prime q has ord_q(2)<=m exactly when q divides P_m=product_{k=1}^m(2^k-1). Since P_m<2^{m(m+1)/2}, it has only O(m^2) distinct prime divisors. Among the first O(m^2)+1 odd primes, at least one therefore does not divide P_m. The standard kth-prime bound q_k=O(k log(k+1)) bounds this selected prime by O(m^2 log(m+2)). For it, ord_p(2)>m; because the order divides p-1, necessarily p>m+1, so p does not divide 2 and p=Omega(n) for n=2m.

results.claim: For S_m=0^m1^m, C_L=L+1 for 1<=L<=m and C_L=2m-L+1 for m
results.proof_sketch: For L<=m, the occurring contents have j=0,...,L trailing ones, giving C_L=L+1. For L>m, every occurrence crosses the unique run boundary and j ranges from L-m through m, giving C_L=2m-L+1. Summation yields D=sum_L C_L=m^2+2m. Exactly the m zero positions and m one positions form unequal unordered pairs, so M=m^2. Since ord_p(2)>m implies p>m+1, max_L C_L=m+1<p. It also gives (2m-1)(p-1)>=(2m-1)(m+1)>=m^2. Thus neither the C_L>p certificate nor the mismatch-count rejection fires, and none of the parent’s p=O(log n), D=O(n log n), or M=O(n log n) regimes applies.

results.claim: On the collision-free instances from the preceding claims, the explicit normalized-state route produces exactly Q=m^2+2m-1=Theta(n^2) distinct records, and the distinct-content route produces D=m^2+2m=Theta(n^2) records. This is a quadratic obstruction to those routes, not a lower bound against every possible algorithm for the open target.
results.proof_sketch: There are 2m-1 positive displacements. At displacement d the mismatch-only route produces one initial state and one state after each of its m_d mismatches. No two such states can agree, because claim 1 would then produce an unequal collision, and no p-mismatch cutoff occurs because m_d<=m<p. Hence Q=sum_d(1+m_d)=(2m-1)+M=m^2+2m-1. The suffix-tree route explicitly creates one record per distinct content, namely D=m^2+2m. Both are quadratic for n=2m even though the input is collision-free and satisfies every condition in the audit’s uncovered regime. An O(n log n) solution could still exploit structure not captured by either enumeration, so no general computational lower bound is asserted.

final_writeup: Let b=Σ and encode symbols canonically as integers. I use F(i,L)=sum_{t=0}^{L-1}s[i+t]b^{L-1-t} mod p; reversing the input handles the opposite coefficient convention. The main structural reduction applies when p does not divide b. For a fixed displacement d between two occurrences, define A_d(k)=sum_{t(n-1)(p-1). A complementary suffix-tree traversal enumerates each distinct substring content once. If D is the total number of distinct substring contents, sorting their (length,fingerprint) pairs takes O(n log n+D). Combining the two routes yields O(n log n+n+min{D,M,n min(n,p)}). This proves the requested O(n log n) bound for several exact regimes: p=O(log n), strings with D=O(n log n), strings with M=O(n log n), and strings having period O(log n). No probabilistic rejection is needed in these regimes. There is a further direct positive certificate that does not require enumerating all D contents. Let C_L be the number of distinct contents of length L. Every trimmed compact-suffix-tree edge spanning string depths a+1 through c contributes one content to each corresponding C_L, so range additions over the O(n) edges compute the entire profile in O(n). If some C_L>p, pigeonhole guarantees two distinct contents with the same residue. Scanning the at most n occurrences of that length, assigning exact content classes with suffix-array/LCP support, and sorting their complete fingerprint and class records constructs a witness in O(n) additional word-RAM time. Thus these instances are solved in O(n log n); in particular D>np is sufficient. If p divides b, every fingerprint reduces to one endpoint character modulo p. Consecutive reversed-prefix comparisons within each residue class solve that entire case in O(n log n). The remaining unresolved regime is p not dividing b, p larger than logarithmic, and strings for which both D and M are superlinear, C_L<=p for every L, and M<=(n-1)(p-1). The normalized-state reduction can still have Θ(n^2) states there, so the argument does not establish the requested worst-case bound. The explicit string 000101 modulo 5 also shows why common reductions to dyadic lengths, monotone length search, or lexicographically adjacent contents cannot close this gap. The obstruction lens shows that this gap is genuinely populated even over a fixed binary alphabet. For S_m=0^m1^m, every length-L content is determined by its number j of trailing ones and has fingerprint 2^j-1. Hence S_m is collision-free modulo an odd prime p exactly when ord_p(2)>m. Such a polynomial-size prime always exists: only O(m^2) odd primes divide product_{k<=m}(2^k-1), and the standard kth-prime bound supplies a nondivisor of size O(m^2 log(m+2)). For this choice, max_L C_L=m+1
